005_26.prose:
The way back down was his own pace now, though his eyes kept going to the fern on either side and over his shoulder to the dark timber above. Nothing crossed the trail. A jay scolded somewhere and went silent as he passed; twice the prints ran beside him in the soft ground, going his way, and twice he was glad of the wind at his back pushing his scent uphill instead of down. The birch thinned, the river noise swelled, and then the trail spilled him out at the treeline with the camp spread below — rafts lashed along the bank, the plank stacks pale in the sun, the dog lifting its head at the wood's edge before it recognized him and dropped its nose again.

Corlin was at the near raft, driving pegs with a mallet, two men fitting a gunwale plank under his direction. He saw Alaric come out of the trees and straightened, laying the mallet on the raft's edge.

"Well?" He came up the bank wiping his hands on the apron. "It's barely past midday. You didn't go far."

Alaric gave it to him plain: a boar down the far slope, but no common boar — big as a yearling ox, dark hide, a ridge of bristle along the spine, old white scars across its flank. Bedded in a hollow over the first bend, the fern flattened and the ground printed deep with clawed tracks. A marked path down to a stream — a pine rubbed smooth and mud-caked at shoulder height, musk laid on musk, seasons of it. It was drinking at that stream when he saw it, and he backed off clean and came away without it ever lifting its head.

Corlin listened with his jaw working, chewing nothing. At the rubbed pine he looked up the hill at the treeline, then back at his stacks.

"Ox-sized." He said it flat, testing the weight of it. "That's not a pig a man bumps into. That's a thing with a routine." He rubbed his thumb along the apron's edge, thinking. "You did right coming off it quiet. A boar that size, wounded, in timber full of men on the ground with saws — no."

He turned and looked down the line of rafts, the wet planks, the mallet lying where he'd left it.

"Here's what I know. That trail's been used longer than my camp. The boys heard rooting some nights and I called it pigs. It kept off the yard, so I let it keep." His mouth set. "Well. Now we know what kept. You're the hired eyes — you tell me what you want done about it. I'll tell you now, I can't spare a day's work to hunt it, and I won't have the men up that hill with axes poking a bed."

005_119.prose:
Corr pulled the table lamp closer and held his hand out flat, palm up, waiting for the goods rather than reaching for them.

The tooth first. He turned it in the light, ran a thumb down the needle of it, sniffed it, and grunted. The strip of hide came next — he stretched it between his fingers, watched how it bent, held it near the flame without touching it. At the word "egg" he stopped and looked up.

"You pulled an egg out of a nest?" His voice had dropped half a tone. "Out from under a live site?"

He laid the tooth and the hide down side by side on the cleared table, careful as a man laying out cutlery, and leaned back with his cup forgotten.

"I'll tell you what I see. Hide and tooth I can buy for the Guild ledger — proof of a kill, name it a fen-lurker or whatever the scribes settle on, that's copper-and-silver work, common enough. Six silver for the pair, and I'd not be robbing you." He tapped the table once. "The egg's different. An egg means a breeding site, and a breeding site means the Guild posts a culling contract and pays proper rates to clear it. That egg is worth more to me as word than as wax — I'll give you a silver for it as a curiosity, no more, because I'm not the one who profits from it."

He sat forward.

"Now, the bigger question you asked. The factor house — Molland's, on the wharf road, blue door — pays for named carcasses, and they'd pay better than me for a whole hide, but you've sold the hide's worth in strips, so they'll not thank you. What they *will* pay for is certainty. There's a woman there, Sarrah Molland, keeps the books, and if you walk in and show her that tooth and tell her there's a nesting site two hours east with a big breeding female walking it, she'll pay silver for the warning — a warning that saves her bargemen a mauling is worth coin to her. The ferry men too, maybe, but they'll buy you a drink and nothing more."

He pushed the tooth and the hide an inch back toward Alaric and folded his hands.

"So. Six silver for tooth and hide, one for the egg, seven silver the lot and I write it in the ledger under a description you give me. Or keep the egg, take the six, and carry your story to Molland's yourself and see what she adds to it." His eyes went to the pouch, where the waxen shape sat. "But understand what you're carrying first. If there's a mother to that egg, she knows it's gone, and the road east runs past her door. That's worth thinking on before you walk it again."

005_121.prose:
Corr pulled the ledger across and dipped his pen — then stopped, pen hovering over the page.

"Wait." He set the pen down and rubbed his jaw. "Let's not muddy the record before it's written. Six silver the lot is me pricing three things blind, and I'd rather do it clean, item by item, the way the ledger wants it."

He laid the tooth and the strip of hide out in a row, considering each in turn, the lamp flame throwing his shadow long across the table.

"Tooth — two silver, and I'll not move on that. Hide — one silver eight, being honest with you that a strip's a strip." He glanced at the pouch. "Egg, one, as I said. That's my numbers, each on its own line."

He looked up and waited, hand flat on the ledger.

"Agree them or argue them, but I need a yes on each before coin moves, because once I write a line in this book it stays written. What's your word on the tooth?"

005_122.prose:
"Tooth at two, written." Corr set the pen to the page and scratched out the line in a quick, practiced hand — *fen-lurker, needle tooth, one* — then flipped open the purse and counted coins onto the wood in two short rows. Two silver, bright against the dark grain.

He slid them across and waited until Alaric's hand had actually closed on them before picking the tooth up off the table and turning it over once more, like a man buying a horse he meant to keep.

"There. First line done." He set the tooth in a small tin beside the lamp and tapped the ledger with the pen's end. "Now the hide. One silver eight for the strip, as I said — and after that the egg at one, and we're finished and you can get your story down to Molland's before the light goes."

Outside, a cart rattled past the window, and someone in the yard shouted at a dog. Corr picked up the strip of waxen hide between two fingers, stretching it against the lamplight again, and looked at Alaric across the table.

"One silver eight. Yes or no?"

inputs.input: I help straighten the cart and gather the spilled turnips, then see to the man's injured arm.
I walk with the cart the rest of the way to the village and take Silla's offer of a seat at the taproom — the stew and bread, if I can pay for my share.
I pay two coppers for my bowl and an ale, eat with Silla and Bones, and ask what they know of the north woods trouble before I see Brenna this evening.
I finish my ale, thank Silla and Bones, and cross the bridge to the mill house to find Brenna, telling her the farmers sent me and asking what she'd pay to have the north woods looked into.
I accept Brenna's offer: I'll go into the north woods in daylight tomorrow, look properly at what's taking the stock, and come back with a true report — three silver, four if I kill it.
"Alaric Red. I'll take the corner room at the taproom, and I'll ask Hedric to walk me to the gate at first light."
I follow the woodcutter's track past the pasture gate, moving slow toward the bend where the ewes were found, watching for tracks or anything out of place.
I step off the track into the hollow and examine the ground closely for tracks or signs of what took the ewes.
I climb up the track toward the old birch stand, watching the trees ahead as I go.
I approach the low, wide shape in the deep shade slowly with my sword ready, and examine it from a few paces without touching it.
I back away quietly without turning my back on the entrance, then watch the opening from cover to see what comes out.

Since nothing emerges and the breathing has settled into deep sleep, I withdraw to the pasture and report to Brenna what I found: a woven bark dome over a breathing den beneath the old birch stand, no kill remains or tracks anywhere.

004_24.prose:
He eases back along the track the way he came, and the stand lets him go without comment. Behind him the breathing under the birch roots keeps its slow ox-pace, asleep or indifferent, and the woodpecker starts up again somewhere as if nothing had ever stopped.

The walk down is quick going, downhill, the ruts firm underfoot where they reappear. The woods thin, the light opens, and the pasture fence comes into view across a stretch of rough grazing, half a mile of it, just as Brenna said. Hedric's pasture lies quiet in the middle of the day: a handful of sheep at the far end, heads down, and near the gate a man mending a hurdle, mallet in hand. He looks up as Alaric comes out of the trees, takes in the sword and the armor, and straightens slowly.

"Looking for the miller?" he says, before anything is asked. "She's been in and out all morning, asking had anything come of the woods. Went down to the village not an hour past." He jerks the mallet toward the track that runs along the pasture's lower edge. "Mill house is twenty minutes, that way, if you're quick."

Brenna is quicker than that. She is already coming up the pasture track on foot as he starts down it—a broad woman with flour worked gray into her forearms and her sleeves rolled to the elbow, walking like someone who does not spare her breath on the road. She stops a few paces off and looks him over, waiting.

He gives it to her plain: the old birch stand, the dome of woven birch bark packed with moss, knee-high and as broad as a haycock, done by hands rather than weather. The opening beneath the roots of the biggest birch. The breathing inside, deep and slow, settled into sleep while he watched. And the strange part—no bones, no dung, no kill-remains anywhere around it, and not a track but deer.

Brenna listens all the way through with her jaw set, and when he finishes she looks past him at the tree line, working something over.

"Nothing dragged in," she says at last, half to him, half to herself. "Then it's not feeding off my ewes where it sleeps. Or it's not the thing that took them at all." She rubs one flour-gray forearm. "Weaves bark like a thatcher, you say. Well." Her eyes come back to him. "There's a question now, isn't there—what it is, and whether it's my thief."
